title: Conjecture 1
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-diameter setting, $A_d=D_d\cap[n]$, and for $D\subseteq[n]$, $m_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{A_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $m_k(n)=m_{[k]}(n)$ for $k\le n$ and $m(n)=m_n(n)$. The authors prove $\left(\frac43-o(1)\right)\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}\le m(n)\le\left(\frac53+o(1)\right)\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$, and suspect that the lower constant $4/3$ is closer to the truth. The lower bound already holds when only prime differences up to $\sqrt n$ are used. In favour of $4/3$, they note that $m_k(n)\le(1.52+o(1))n^{3/2}/\ln n$ for $k\le\sqrt n$ and $m_k(n)=(1+o(1))kn/\ln k$ for $k\ll\sqrt n$. Pinning down the exact constant seems to require additional ideas. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Conjecture 2
context_text: Theorem 2 establishes $M(n)=\Theta(n^3/\ln n)$ with lower constant $1/6$ and upper constant approximately $0.526$. The authors suspect $1/6$ is the correct multiplicative factor for the fixed-size variant $M_n(n)$.

title: Conjecture 3
context_text: The authors describe these prime-restricted conjectures as 'apparently much weaker' than Conjectures 1–2, viewing understanding primes as a key step towards solving more general settings. Here $\mathbb{P}(x)$ denotes the set of primes not exceeding $x$.

title: Conjecture 4
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-size setting, $B_d=\{d,2d,\dots,nd\}$ (the first $n$ multiples of $d$), and for a set $D$ of positive integers, $M_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{B_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $M_k(n)=M_{[k]}(n)$ (defined for every $k$) and $M(n)=M_n(n)$. Here $\mathbb{P}(x)$ denotes the set of primes not exceeding $x$, so the conjecture concerns packing the progressions $\{p,2p,\dots,np\}$ for all primes $p\le n$. The authors prove $\left(\frac16-o(1)\right)\frac{n^3}{\ln n}\le M(n)\le(0.526+o(1))\frac{n^3}{\ln n}$ and conjecture $M(n)\sim\frac16\frac{n^3}{\ln n}$. They view the prime-only versions, this one and the analogous $m_{\mathbb{P}(\sqrt n)}(n)\sim\frac43\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$ (where $m_D(n)$ packs the sets $D_d\cap[n]$, $d\in D$), as apparently much weaker but key to understanding the general setting, and as closely related to each other. The lower bound in this conjecture follows from the proof of their lower bound for $M_k(n)$; the upper bound is open. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: For every $k$ satisfying $\Omega(\sqrt{n})=k<\sqrt{n}$, we have $m_{k}(n)\sim\left(1-\frac{k^{2}}{3n}\right)\frac{k}{\ln k}\cdot n$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-diameter setting, $A_d=D_d\cap[n]$, and for $D\subseteq[n]$, $m_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{A_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $m_k(n)=m_{[k]}(n)$ for $k\le n$ and $m(n)=m_n(n)$. The authors prove that $m(n)=\Theta(n^{3/2}/\ln n)$ (with constants between $4/3$ and $5/3$) and conjecture $m(n)\sim\frac43\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$. For $k\le\sqrt n$ they show $m_k(n)=(1+o(1))kn/\ln k$ when $k\ll\sqrt n$, and $\left(1-\frac{k^2}{3n}-o(1)\right)\frac{kn}{\ln k}\le m_k(n)\le\left(1-\frac{k^2}{3n}+\frac{k^2}{48n}+o(1)\right)\frac{kn}{\ln k}$ when $k\le\sqrt{n/2}$, with a weaker upper bound for $\sqrt{n/2}\le k\le\sqrt n$. If $m(n)\sim\frac43\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$ holds, this also settles $m_k(n)$ asymptotically for $k\ge\sqrt n$, so the only remaining case is $k<\sqrt n$ with $k$ not $o(\sqrt n)$, which this conjecture addresses (the conjectured value is the lower bound). This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Conjecture 6
statement_text: If $k\ll n$, then $M_{k}(n)\sim\frac{k^{2}}{2\ln k}\cdot n$, while otherwise, $M_{k}(n)\sim\frac{k^{2}}{2\ln k}\cdot n-\frac{k^{3}}{3\ln k}$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-size setting, $B_d=\{d,2d,\dots,nd\}$ (the first $n$ multiples of $d$), and for a set $D$ of positive integers, $M_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{B_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $M_k(n)=M_{[k]}(n)$ (defined for every $k$) and $M(n)=M_n(n)$. For $k\le n$ the authors prove that $\left(\frac12-o(1)\right)\frac{k^2n}{\ln k}\le M_k(n)\le\left(\frac{\zeta(2)}{2}+o(1)\right)\frac{k^2n}{\ln k}$ when $k\ll n$, and $\left(\frac12-\frac{k}{3n}-o(1)\right)\frac{k^2n}{\ln k}\le M_k(n)$ in general, with corresponding upper bounds involving $\zeta(2)$ and $\zeta(3)$. The conjecture asserts that the lower bounds are asymptotically tight in both regimes, $k\ll n$ and $k$ of order $n$ (with $k<n$). In particular for $k=n$ it gives $M(n)\sim\frac16\frac{n^3}{\ln n}$, also conjectured separately. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: For every fixed $n$ and $k$ tending to infinity, we have $M_{k}(n)=(1+o(1))nk$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-size setting, $B_d=\{d,2d,\dots,nd\}$ (the first $n$ multiples of $d$), and for a set $D$ of positive integers, $M_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{B_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $M_k(n)=M_{[k]}(n)$ (defined for every $k$) and $M(n)=M_n(n)$. Since the $k$ progressions have $n$ elements each, $M_k(n)\ge nk$ trivially. The authors prove that for every $n$ there is $k_0(n)$ with $M_k(n)\le3nk$ for all $k\ge k_0$, using a hypergraph matching argument: for every $\epsilon>0$ and $k$ large, at least $(1-\epsilon)k$ of the progressions $B_1,\dots,B_k$ can be packed into the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{nk}$. They suspect that the trivial lower bound is asymptotically correct. Such a bound may fail for general families of $n$-element sets: $k$ copies of $\{1,\dots,r,2r,3r,\dots,(r+1)r\}$ (with $n=2r$) need an interval of length $\Omega(kn^2)$. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
